column2:
(v) to praise highly
Critics lauded the film as the best of the decade, and it won every major award.
Syn: extol, acclaim

(v) to praise enthusiastically
The coach extolled her players' discipline in every interview and never missed a chance to praise them.
Syn: laud, acclaim

(v) to regard with deep respect
The villagers venerate the old teacher and still seek her advice on every important matter.
Syn: revere

(v) to respect and admire deeply
Students revered the professor so much that they fell silent whenever he entered the room.
Syn: venerate

(n, v) enthusiastic public praise; to praise publicly
The novel won wide acclaim, with reviewers calling it a masterpiece.
Syn: laud, approbation

(n) excessive admiration or praise
The singer grew tired of the adulation of fans who screamed at everything he did.
Syn: flattery, worship

(v, n) to criticize formally and strongly (not censor)
The senate voted to censure the minister for misleading the public.
Syn: rebuke, reproach

(v) to criticize or punish severely
The editor castigated the reporter for publishing the story without checking a single fact.
Syn: lambaste, berate

(v) to scold angrily and at length
The manager berated the waiter in front of customers for dropping one plate.
Syn: upbraid, castigate

(v, n) to criticize sharply; a sharp criticism
The judge rebuked the lawyer for interrupting the witness yet again.
Syn: reproach, admonish

(v) to scold or punish
She chastised her son for lying and took away his phone for a week.
Syn: rebuke, castigate

(v) to warn or scold gently but firmly
The librarian admonished the children to keep their voices down.
Syn: rebuke, reproach

(v) to speak of as having little worth
He disparaged his rival's research, calling it shallow and unoriginal.
Syn: belittle, denigrate

(v) to attack the reputation of unfairly
The campaign tried to denigrate the candidate by spreading rumors about her past.
Syn: disparage, vilify

(v) to mock with contempt
Early critics derided the invention as a useless toy and laughed at its inventor.
Syn: scorn, ridicule

(v) to make seem small or unimportant
She belittled his promotion by saying that anyone could have got it.
Syn: disparage

(v) to describe as evil; to slander
The press vilified the banker as a greedy villain long before the trial began.
Syn: denigrate

(v) to criticize harshly
Reviewers lambasted the sequel, calling it lazy, dull and far too long.
Syn: castigate, excoriate

(v, n) to express disappointment or blame
She reproached him for forgetting her birthday, though she sounded more hurt than angry.
Syn: rebuke, admonish

(v) to scold severely
The captain upbraided the sailor for sleeping on watch.
Syn: berate, chastise

(adj) talking too much, often about trivial things
Our garrulous neighbor kept us at the gate for an hour with stories about his cats.
Syn: loquacious, voluble

(adj) very talkative
The normally loquacious host fell silent when asked about the scandal.
Syn: garrulous, voluble

(adj) using more words than needed
The verbose report took ten pages to say what one paragraph could have said.
Syn: prolix

(adj) talking fluently and rapidly
A voluble salesman, he could talk for minutes without pausing for breath.
Syn: loquacious, garrulous

(adj) tediously long and wordy
Readers gave up on the prolix novel, which spent fifty pages describing a single dinner.
Syn: verbose

(adj) expressing feelings in an unrestrained way
Her effusive thanks, repeated five times with hugs, embarrassed the shy doctor.
Syn: gushing, fulsome

(adj) sounding grand but with little meaning
The bombastic speech was full of grand phrases and empty of actual plans.
Syn: pompous

(n) an indirect, roundabout way of speaking
Tired of the minister's circumlocution, the reporter demanded a simple yes or no.
Syn: wordiness, evasion

(v) to wander from the main topic
The lecturer often digressed into stories about his travels and never finished the syllabus.
Syn: stray, deviate

(adj) fluent and persuasive in speech or writing
Her eloquent plea moved the jury to tears and changed the verdict.
Syn: articulate

(adj) habitually saying very little
The taciturn farmer answered every question with a nod or a single word.
Syn: reticent, laconic

(adj) unwilling to speak freely; reserved
He was reticent about his childhood and changed the subject whenever it came up.
Syn: taciturn

(adj) using very few words
Her laconic reply, a single "No," ended the two-hour debate.
Syn: terse, taciturn

(adj) brief, sometimes to the point of rudeness
His terse email, just three words long, made her nervous.
Syn: curt, laconic

(adj) briefly and clearly expressed
The summary was succinct and covered the whole project in three clear sentences.
Syn: concise, pithy

(adj) giving much information in few words
Keep your answer concise, because the examiner has only a minute to read it.
Syn: succinct

(adj) short and full of meaning
The essay ended with a pithy remark that readers quoted for years.
Syn: succinct

(adj) rudely brief
Offended by her curt "Not now," he left without saying goodbye.
Syn: brusque, terse

(adj) abrupt and blunt in manner
The doctor's brusque manner upset patients, who felt rushed and unheard.
Syn: curt

(n) shortness of expression or of time
The speech was praised for its brevity, as it lasted barely two minutes.
Syn: concision

(adj) stubbornly refusing to change one's mind
The obstinate child refused to wear a coat even as snow began to fall.
Syn: obdurate, intransigent

(adj) stubbornly unmoved by persuasion or pity
The landlord remained obdurate and ignored the family's pleas for one more week.
Syn: obstinate

(adj) refusing to compromise
Talks collapsed because both sides were intransigent and would not give up a single demand.
Syn: obdurate, adamant

(adj) stubbornly resisting authority or control
The recalcitrant student ignored every rule the school tried to enforce.
Syn: intractable, insubordinate

(adj) hard to control, manage or solve
The disease proved intractable and resisted every treatment the doctors tried.
Syn: recalcitrant

(adj) holding firmly; not giving up easily
The tenacious reporter chased the story for three years until she had proof.
Syn: dogged, resolute

(adj) persistent in spite of difficulty
Through dogged effort, he passed the exam on his fifth attempt.
Syn: tenacious

(adj) refusing to be persuaded
She was adamant that she would not sign, whatever they offered her.
Syn: intransigent, resolute

(adj) firmly loyal and unchanging
He remained a steadfast friend when everyone else had abandoned her.
Syn: resolute, abiding

(adj) firmly determined
Resolute in her decision to leave, she ignored every attempt to change her mind.
Syn: steadfast, adamant

(adj) stating opinions as certain truths, without evidence
The dogmatic professor dismissed any theory that differed from his own.
Syn: opinionated, doctrinaire

(adj) easily bent or influenced
The young recruits were pliable and accepted whatever the leader told them.
Syn: malleable

(adj) easily shaped or influenced
Children's minds are malleable, so early teaching leaves a lasting mark.
Syn: pliable

(adj) easy to control or deal with
The new horse was tractable and followed commands from the first day.
Syn: docile, amenable

(adj) willing to accept a suggestion
The manager was amenable to the change and approved it at once.
Syn: tractable, compliant

(adj) quiet and easy to control
The once wild dog became docile after months of patient training.
Syn: tractable, meek

(adj) willing to obey rules or requests
Compliant employees followed the new policy without a single complaint.
Syn: amenable, docile

(v) to accept reluctantly without protest
Though she disliked the plan, she acquiesced rather than start another argument.
Syn: concede, capitulate

(v) to stop resisting; to surrender
After a week of strikes, the company capitulated and raised wages.
Syn: acquiesce

(v) to admit something is true; to give up
He finally conceded that his opponent had the stronger argument.
Syn: acquiesce

(n) deliberate deceit; double-dealing
His duplicity was exposed when both partners found he had promised each of them the same contract.
Syn: guile

(n) clever, sly deception
She used guile rather than force and tricked the guard into opening the door.
Syn: duplicity, cunning

(adj) not sincere; pretending to know less than one does
It was disingenuous of him to act surprised at news he had leaked himself.
Syn: insincere

(adj) lying; untruthful
The mendacious witness changed his story three times under oath.
Syn: dishonest

(adj) false or fake, though seeming genuine
The claim rested on spurious data that no other laboratory could reproduce.
Syn: specious, bogus

(adj) seeming right or true but actually false
The argument sounded convincing but was specious, since it ignored half the evidence.
Syn: fallacious, spurious

(adj) based on a mistaken belief or bad logic
It is fallacious to assume that because two events occur together, one causes the other.
Syn: specious

(v) to pretend to feel or have
He feigned illness to avoid the meeting and coughed loudly on the phone.
Syn: dissemble, fake

(v) to hide one's real feelings or intentions
Unable to dissemble, she let her disappointment show plainly on her face.
Syn: feign

(v) to avoid telling the truth by being evasive
Asked directly whether he took the money, he prevaricated and talked about his busy week.
Syn: equivocate

(v) to use vague language to avoid commitment
The candidate equivocated on taxes, giving answers that could mean anything.
Syn: prevaricate

(n) a person falsely claiming skill or knowledge
The so-called healer was a charlatan who sold colored water as medicine.
Syn: fraud, quack

(v) to invent in order to deceive
The researcher fabricated results for experiments he had never run.
Syn: concoct

(adj) honest and direct
In a candid interview, she admitted the mistakes she had made as leader.
Syn: forthright, frank

(adj) direct and outspoken
He gave a forthright answer and said plainly that the plan would fail.
Syn: candid

(adj) innocent, trusting and sincere (not ingenious)
Her ingenuous belief that everyone tells the truth made her easy to fool.
Syn: artless, guileless

(adj) natural and sincere; without deceit
The child's artless question, asked with no hidden motive, embarrassed the adults.
Syn: ingenuous, guileless

(n) truthfulness; accuracy
Reporters questioned the veracity of the statement after documents contradicted it.
Syn: truthfulness

(adj) honest and without cunning
Guileless and open, he never suspected that his partners were cheating him.
Syn: artless, ingenuous

(adj) very careful to do what is right; very thorough
A scrupulous accountant, she reported even the smallest error in her own favor.
Syn: conscientious, meticulous

(adj) likely to change suddenly
Prices were so volatile that a stock could double and halve in the same week.
Syn: erratic, mercurial

(adj) changing mood or behavior without reason
The capricious director praised a scene one day and cut it the next.
Syn: fickle, whimsical

(adj) quickly changing in mood
Her mercurial temper meant that laughter could turn to rage within minutes.
Syn: volatile, capricious

(adj) changing loyalties or interests often
Fickle fans who cheered the team last year now boo it after two losses.
Syn: capricious

(adj) irregular and unpredictable
The driver's erratic steering, swerving left and right, alarmed the police.
Syn: volatile

(adj) playfully fanciful; decided by sudden impulse
On a whimsical impulse, he painted the front door bright purple.
Syn: capricious

(v) to keep changing between opinions
She vacillated for weeks between the two job offers, unable to choose.
Syn: waver

(v) to become unsteady or undecided
His confidence wavered when he saw how difficult the first question was.
Syn: vacillate

(v) to rise and fall irregularly
Temperatures fluctuate widely in the desert, from freezing nights to burning days.
Syn: vary

(adj) liable to change
Fashion is mutable, and what is admired today looks silly in a decade.
Syn: changeable

(adj) lasting only a short time
The pain was transient and had disappeared by the next morning.
Syn: ephemeral, fleeting

(adj) lasting a very short time
Fame on the internet is ephemeral, and last month's star is already forgotten.
Syn: transient, fleeting

(adj) passing very quickly
She caught only a fleeting glimpse of the bird before it vanished.
Syn: transient, ephemeral

(adj) not permanent
He reminded himself that the hardship was transitory and that better days would come.
Syn: transient

(adj) not moving or changing
Wages remained static for five years while prices kept rising.
Syn: stagnant

(adj) unable to be changed
The laws of physics are immutable, whatever politicians may wish.
Syn: unchangeable

(adj) not flowing, growing or developing
The stagnant economy produced no new jobs for three years.
Syn: static

(adj) lasting or recurring for a long time
Traffic is a perennial problem in the city, complained about by every generation.
Syn: abiding, enduring

(adj) lasting a long time
Her abiding love of music stayed with her from childhood to old age.
Syn: steadfast, perennial

(adj) firmly established and hard to change
The habit was so entrenched that no campaign could persuade people to give it up.
Syn: ingrained

(v) to make a bad situation better
New housing helped ameliorate the overcrowding in the city center.
Syn: alleviate, mitigate

(v) to make pain or a problem less severe
The medicine alleviated her headache within minutes.
Syn: mitigate, assuage

(v) to make less severe or harmful
Planting trees can mitigate the effects of flooding.
Syn: alleviate

(v) to ease an unpleasant feeling
Nothing could assuage his guilt over the accident.
Syn: allay, alleviate

(v) to calm someone's anger
The airline tried to mollify angry passengers with free meals.
Syn: placate, appease

(v) to make less angry, often by giving in
He placated the crying child with a promise of ice cream.
Syn: mollify, appease

(v) to calm by giving what is demanded
The king appeased the rebels by lowering their taxes.
Syn: placate

(v) to bring calm or peace to
Police were sent to pacify the crowd before the protest turned violent.
Syn: mollify

(v) to reduce fear, doubt or worry
The pilot's calm announcement allayed the passengers' fears.
Syn: assuage

(v) to win over; to end a disagreement peacefully
The manager tried to conciliate the two departments by meeting the concerns of each.
Syn: placate, appease

(v) to support or strengthen
The new evidence bolstered her case and convinced the doubtful jurors.
Syn: buttress

(v, n) to support or strengthen; a support
He buttressed his argument with statistics from three separate studies.
Syn: bolster

(v) to make a bad situation worse
Shouting at the frightened dog only exacerbated its aggression.
Syn: aggravate, compound

(v) to make worse
Running on the injured ankle aggravated the damage.
Syn: exacerbate

(v) to make worse by adding to (second meaning)
He compounded the error by lying about it afterwards.
Syn: exacerbate, aggravate

(v) to weaken gradually or secretly
Constant criticism undermined her confidence until she stopped speaking in meetings.
Syn: impair, erode

(v) to damage or weaken
Lack of sleep impairs memory and slows reaction time.
Syn: undermine

(v) to make very weak
The long illness debilitated him so much that he could barely stand.
Syn: enervate

(v) to drain of energy; to weaken (not energize)
The humid heat enervated the hikers, who could hardly lift their feet by noon.
Syn: debilitate

(v) to spoil or reduce the value of
One false figure vitiated the whole study and made its conclusions worthless.
Syn: impair, undermine

(adj) clear and easy to understand
Her lucid explanation made even quantum physics seem simple.
Syn: coherent, clear

(adj) stated clearly, leaving no doubt
The contract was explicit that payment was due on the first of each month.
Syn: unequivocal

(adj) leaving no doubt; not ambiguous
The answer was an unequivocal no, with no room for negotiation.
Syn: explicit

(adj) clear, logical and convincing
She made such a cogent case that even her opponents voted for the plan.
Syn: compelling

(adj) logical and consistent; easy to follow
After the accident he was too confused to give a coherent account of events.
Syn: lucid

(v) to make clear; to explain
The diagram helped elucidate a process that words alone had left confusing.
Syn: explicate

(v) to explain in detail
The scholar spent a chapter explicating a single line of the poem.
Syn: elucidate

(adj, v) clearly visible; to show clearly
His relief was manifest in the broad smile that spread across his face.
Syn: patent, evince

(adj) having more than one possible meaning
The ambiguous sign left drivers unsure whether the road was closed or open.
Syn: equivocal

(adj) deliberately unclear; open to two readings
His equivocal reply let both sides believe that he supported them.
Syn: ambiguous

(adj, v) little known; hard to understand; to hide
The poem's meaning remained obscure even to experts who studied it for years.
Syn: opaque, abstruse

(adj) not transparent; hard to understand
The legal language was so opaque that no ordinary reader could follow it.
Syn: obscure

(adj) difficult to understand
The lecture was so abstruse that only two specialists in the audience followed it.
Syn: arcane, esoteric

(adj) known or understood by very few
He loved the arcane rules of medieval heraldry, which almost nobody else had studied.
Syn: esoteric

(adj) meant for a small group with special knowledge
The journal publishes esoteric papers that only a handful of mathematicians can read.
Syn: arcane, abstruse

(adj) mysterious; having a hidden meaning
She left a cryptic note of three words that nobody could explain.
Syn: enigmatic

(adj) puzzling; hard to interpret
His enigmatic smile gave no hint of whether he was pleased or angry.
Syn: cryptic

(adj) vague; without clear form
The plan was still nebulous, with no dates, costs or names attached.
Syn: vague

(adj) extremely complicated and hard to follow
The plot was so convoluted that viewers needed a chart to track who had betrayed whom.
Syn: tortuous

(v) to make unclear on purpose
The company used technical jargon to obfuscate the real cost of the loan.
Syn: obscure

(adj) proud and looking down on others
The haughty duchess refused to speak to the servants directly.
Syn: supercilious, imperious

(adj) behaving as if superior to others
With a supercilious lift of his eyebrow, the waiter corrected my pronunciation.
Syn: haughty, condescending

(adj) treating others as less intelligent
His condescending tone, as if he were explaining to a child, annoyed the experienced engineers.
Syn: patronizing

(adj) kind in a way that shows a sense of superiority
She gave him a patronizing pat on the head and told him it was a good try.
Syn: condescending

(adj) self-important and overly grand
The pompous official insisted on being addressed by his full title at all times.
Syn: pretentious, bombastic

(adj) trying to seem more important or cultured than one is
The pretentious menu described plain toast as artisan grilled bread.
Syn: pompous

(n) excessive pride that leads to a fall
In his hubris, the general ignored every warning and marched his army into the trap.
Syn: arrogance

(adj) arrogantly giving orders
With an imperious wave of her hand, she dismissed the whole committee.
Syn: haughty

(n, v) the feeling that something is unworthy of respect
She looked at the cheap gift with disdain and pushed it aside.
Syn: scorn, contempt

(n, v) open contempt; to reject with contempt
The scientist scorned the idea and called it childish nonsense.
Syn: disdain, deride

(adj) showing a strong lack of respect
His contemptuous laugh made it clear what he thought of their proposal.
Syn: scornful, disdainful

(adj) distant and not friendly
She stayed aloof at parties and stood alone by the window.
Syn: detached, reserved

(adj) too satisfied with oneself to notice danger
Complacent after years of success, the firm ignored its new competitors until it was too late.
Syn: smug

(adj) shy because of a lack of confidence
Too diffident to raise his hand, he let others answer questions he knew well.
Syn: meek, self-effacing

(adj) not drawing attention to oneself; modest
The self-effacing winner gave all the credit to her team.
Syn: unassuming

(adj) modest; not showy
Despite his fame, he lived in an unassuming house and drove an old car.
Syn: self-effacing

(adj) showing polite respect
The young lawyer was deferential to the judge and never once interrupted.
Syn: respectful

(adj) quiet, gentle and easily imposed on
Too meek to complain, he ate the cold meal without a word.
Syn: docile, diffident

(adj) quiet, modest and reserved
She gave a demure smile and lowered her eyes when praised.
Syn: modest

(v) to lower in rank or dignity; to humble
He refused to abase himself by begging his former employee for a job.
Syn: humble, demean

(adj) wealthy
The affluent suburb was full of large houses and expensive cars.
Syn: opulent

(adj) rich and luxurious
The opulent palace had gold ceilings and marble floors.
Syn: lavish

(adj, v) rich and generous; to give in large amounts
They held a lavish wedding with a thousand guests and a ten-course dinner.
Syn: opulent, extravagant

(adj) wastefully extravagant with money
The prodigal heir spent his entire inheritance in two years.
Syn: profligate, spendthrift

(adj) recklessly wasteful; also immoral
The profligate government borrowed billions for projects nobody needed.
Syn: prodigal

(adj) spending or costing far too much
Buying a third sports car seemed extravagant even to his rich friends.
Syn: lavish, prodigal

(n) a person who wastes money
A spendthrift by nature, he was broke a week after every payday.
Syn: prodigal, profligate

(adj) extremely generous
A munificent donor paid for the entire new hospital wing.
Syn: magnanimous

(adj) generous and forgiving, especially to a rival
Magnanimous in victory, she praised the campaign of her defeated opponent.
Syn: munificent

(v) to waste foolishly
He squandered his savings on lottery tickets.
Syn: waste, fritter

(adj) careful with money; economical
A frugal student, she cooked at home and walked everywhere to save money.
Syn: thrifty

(adj) using money carefully
Thrifty shoppers wait for the sales before buying winter coats.
Syn: frugal

(adj) extremely unwilling to spend money
The parsimonious owner refused to heat the office even in January.
Syn: miserly

(adj) hating to spend money; stingy
The miserly old man kept a fortune in the bank while wearing torn shoes.
Syn: parsimonious

(adj) severely plain; strict and without comfort
The monk's austere room held only a bed, a chair and a candle.
Syn: spartan, stark

(adj) very poor; needy
The clinic offers free care to indigent patients who cannot pay.
Syn: destitute, impoverished

(adj) without money, food or a home
The fire left the family destitute, with nothing but the clothes they wore.
Syn: indigent

(adj) made poor; weakened
Drought impoverished the farmers, who had to sell their land.
Syn: indigent

(n) extreme greed for wealth
Driven by avarice, the banker risked his clients' savings for a larger bonus.
Syn: greed

(adj) able to pay one's debts
The loan kept the company solvent through a year of falling sales.
Syn: creditworthy

(v) to limit or soften a statement
She qualified her praise by adding that the plan still had serious gaps.
Syn: temper, modify

(v) to postpone discussion of (US usage)
The committee tabled the proposal until next year, so no vote was taken.
Syn: shelve, defer

(v) to grow tired or weaker
After six hours of climbing, their energy began to flag and the pace slowed.
Syn: wane

(v, n) to stop or restrain; a restraint
The new law was designed to check the growth of monopolies.
Syn: stem, curtail

(v) to stop or slow a process; to catch attention
The drug arrested the spread of the infection within days.
Syn: check, stem

(n, v) a lack; to lack
The project failed for want of funds, not for want of effort.
Syn: dearth, paucity

(v) to make less extreme; to moderate
He tempered his criticism with a few kind words about her effort.
Syn: qualify, mitigate

(v, n) to approve officially; also a penalty
The board sanctioned the merger, so the deal could finally go ahead.
Syn: authorize, endorse

(v) to take for one's own use, often without permission
The general appropriated the villagers' grain to feed his army.
Syn: seize, commandeer

(v) to hint or suggest indirectly
She intimated that she might resign, though she never said so directly.
Syn: insinuate, allude

(v) to demand and obtain by force or authority
The gang exacted payment from every shopkeeper on the street.
Syn: extort, demand

(v) to support or defend a cause
The senator championed the rights of workers throughout her career.
Syn: advocate, espouse

(adj) dull and ordinary
The film's pedestrian plot offered nothing that viewers had not seen a hundred times.
Syn: prosaic, mundane

(adj) obvious; plain to see
It was a patent lie, since everyone had watched him take the money.
Syn: manifest, blatant

(adj) having fine judgment or taste
A discriminating reader, she could tell a great novel from a merely good one.
Syn: discerning

(v) to offer formally
The minister tendered his resignation the morning after the scandal broke.
Syn: offer, submit

(v) to use carefully and sparingly
Lost in the desert, they husbanded their water and drank only a sip an hour.
Syn: conserve

(v) to try to win favor; to risk inviting something bad
By ignoring the safety rules, the climbers were courting disaster.
Syn: invite, woo

(v) to stop the flow of; also stem from = to come from
Nurses pressed on the wound to stem the bleeding.
Syn: check, arrest

(v) to come safely through a difficulty
The small shop weathered the recession and even grew afterwards.
Syn: withstand, endure

(adj) hard-working and persistent
Assiduous practice, three hours every day, made her the best pianist in the school.
Syn: diligent, industrious

(adj) steady and careful in work
A diligent student, he reviewed his notes after every class.
Syn: assiduous

(adj) hard-working
The industrious ants carried food to the nest from dawn to dusk.
Syn: diligent

(adj) never getting tired
An indefatigable campaigner, she knocked on doors for twelve hours a day.
Syn: tireless, tenacious

(adj) very careful about small details
The meticulous editor checked every comma in the 600-page book.
Syn: fastidious, painstaking

(adj) very fussy about detail or cleanliness
Fastidious about hygiene, he washed his hands after touching any door handle.
Syn: meticulous

(adj) done with great care and effort
After years of painstaking research, she finally traced the author of the letter.
Syn: meticulous

(adj) wishing to do one's work well and thoroughly
The conscientious nurse double-checked every dose before giving it.
Syn: diligent, scrupulous

(adj) full of eager enthusiasm for a cause
Zealous volunteers worked through the night to finish the shelter.
Syn: ardent, fervent

(adj) passionate; very enthusiastic
An ardent supporter of the team, he had not missed a match in twenty years.
Syn: fervent, zealous

(adj) showing strong, sincere feeling
She made a fervent appeal for donations, her voice shaking with emotion.
Syn: ardent

(adj) lacking energy; sluggish
The heavy lunch left everyone lethargic and yawning through the afternoon meeting.
Syn: languid, listless

(adj) lazy; avoiding effort
The indolent clerk let papers pile up for weeks rather than file them.
Syn: lazy, slothful

(adj) showing no interest or concern
Apathetic voters stayed home and said the result made no difference to them.
Syn: indifferent, listless

(adj) slow and relaxed; lacking energy
With a languid wave from her deckchair, she sent the waiter for another drink.
Syn: lethargic

(adj) having no energy or enthusiasm
The fever left the child listless and uninterested even in her favorite toys.
Syn: lethargic, languid

(adj) done quickly as a duty, without care
The guard gave our bags a perfunctory glance and waved us through.
Syn: cursory

(adj) quick and not thorough
A cursory reading missed the error that a careful one would have caught.
Syn: perfunctory

(adj) failing to take proper care
The negligent driver was texting when he hit the cyclist.
Syn: remiss

(adj) careless in doing one's duty
It was remiss of me not to thank you earlier for your help.
Syn: negligent

(adj) causing argument; fond of arguing
The contentious issue of school fees split the council for months.
Syn: controversial, polemical

(adj) hostile and ready to fight
The belligerent customer shouted at staff and threatened to break the window.
Syn: bellicose, pugnacious

(adj) eager to fight or go to war
The bellicose speech, full of threats, alarmed neighboring countries.
Syn: belligerent

(adj) quick to argue or fight
The pugnacious player was sent off for starting a third brawl.
Syn: belligerent, truculent

(adj) aggressively defiant
The truculent teenager met every request with a glare and a refusal.
Syn: pugnacious

(adj) strongly attacking an opinion in argument
His polemical essay attacked the policy line by line and spared no one.
Syn: contentious

(v) to make someone hostile
Her constant corrections antagonized colleagues who had once liked her.
Syn: alienate, provoke

(n) strong hostility
The animosity between the brothers was so strong that they had not spoken in ten years.
Syn: enmity, rancor

(n) deep, lasting hatred between people
Decades of enmity between the clans ended with a marriage.
